instructions: 문학적 미스터리 판타지 소설. 지문은 자연스러운 한국어 ~다 문체. 은유의 뜻, 행위 주체, 부정, 시간 순서와 단서를 보존한다. 대사는 한국어 소설처럼 자연스럽게 쓰되 관계를 지어내지 않는다. Nara는 성인 수리공, Jun은 소년이며 Nara와 친하다. Jun은 Nara에게 존댓말, Nara는 Jun에게 반말. Nara와 노인 Elias는 처음 만난 사이로 서로 존댓말을 쓴다. 인물 이름과 별명·직함은 구별한다. 고유명사의 한국어 표기는 모델이 원문 근거로 정하고 이후 모든 회차에 같은 기준을 적용한다. 숫자, 소유 관계, 생사와 선택을 바꾸지 않는다. 요약하거나 설명을 덧붙이지 않는다.

documents.title: 01화 · 울리지 않는 종
paragraphs: By the time Nara Reed reached the bell tower, the fog had swallowed the roofs of Greyhaven. Only the harbor lamps remained, small amber wounds in the dark. Her father had repaired those lamps before he disappeared. Every autumn she found another of his initials beneath a brass fitting, and every autumn she pretended it was a message left for her rather than the ordinary vanity of a careful craftsman.

Jun waited on the stairs with a parcel pressed beneath his coat. Rain ran from his hair onto the wrapping. 'I didn't steal it,' he said before she asked. 'Mrs. Vale told me to bring it to you. She said your father would have known what to do.' Nara took the parcel, but not his excuse. 'Then why are you shaking?' The boy looked toward the harbor. 'Because the woman who gave it to me died last winter.'

Inside lay a tideglass, no larger than a plum, and a folded page from the Grey Register. Nara remembered the instrument from her father's workbench. Its blue needle measured the water waiting beneath the city, not the water already in the streets. Tonight the needle pointed upward. On the page, beneath the name Tomas Reed, someone had written: RETURNED. The date was tomorrow's.

'Wait in my shop,' Nara told Jun. 'Keep the stove lit. If anyone asks where I went, say you don't know.' 'I do know.' 'Then learn to be less helpful.' He tried to smile and failed. Before he left, she put her dry scarf around his neck. For a moment the stairs smelled of soot and orange peel, the familiar smell of a winter that had not yet arrived.

The tower door opened before she knocked. An old man stood beyond it, holding a lamp without a flame. 'Elias Ward,' he said. 'They usually call me the Ferryman.' 'I haven't come for a boat, Mr. Ward.' 'No. You have come for a name.' His eyes moved to the tideglass in her hand. Nara closed her fingers over it. 'Did you know my father?' 'I knew what he refused to do.'

Above them hung the Mourning Bell, green with salt and silent for twelve years. Its rope had been cut, yet a wet mark crossed the floor beneath it. Elias turned the lamp so that she could see two iron keys inside the empty bowl. 'The Harbor Council locked the lower archive after the flood. Your father kept the other key.' Nara touched the chain at her throat. She had worn his key for twelve years without finding a lock it would open.

Elias led her down a passage where the walls sweated cold water. Behind an iron door, the Grey Register rested on a desk bolted to the floor. Names filled its pages in the same narrow handwriting. Beside each name stood a date; beside some stood a price. Nara found her father's entry. Under RETURNED, in ink still shining, the book had added a second line: ONE NAME MUST TAKE HIS PLACE.

She reached for the page. Elias caught her wrist, gently enough that she could have pulled away. 'Read the margin first.' There, almost hidden beneath the binding, Tomas had left a sentence in his untidy hand: A borrowed voice is not a living man. Somewhere under the floor, something knocked three times. Then it spoke with her father's voice. 'Nara. Please open the door.'

documents.title: 02화 · 장부의 빈자리
paragraphs: Nara did not open the door. She counted the knocks again in her head, as if counting could make them ordinary. Her father had always knocked twice, once with his knuckle and once with the heel of his hand. The voice below knew her name, but it did not know how he had announced himself. Elias released her wrist. 'Most people stop reading when the book promises them what they want,' he said.

The Grey Register was not a list of the dead. It was an agreement. After the flood, the Harbor Council had offered the city a borrowed year: dry streets, safe boats, lamps that would not go out. The price was a name at every autumn tide. A person whose name was surrendered would disappear from the memories of everyone who had loved them. Tomas Reed had discovered the price and broken the mechanism that chose the next name.

'You expect me to believe a book can take a person?' Nara asked. Elias set his unlit lamp on the desk. 'My wife's name was Ada. I know that because I wrote it on the inside of my wedding ring. I do not remember her face.' His voice remained level. That was worse than grief. Nara thought of the marks beneath the harbor lamps and wondered whether her father had been leaving messages after all.

Jun appeared at the passage entrance, breathless. 'I kept the stove lit,' he said. 'Then Mrs. Vale came back. She asked whether you'd read the whole page.' Nara wanted to scold him for following her. Instead she asked what the woman had looked like. 'Like herself,' he said. 'Except the rain went through her coat.' He offered a damp envelope. Inside was another iron key, tied to a thread of red wool.

There were three iron keys now, but only two locks on the archive door. Elias examined the new key without touching the wool. 'The third opens the bell's heart.' 'Why didn't you tell me there was a third?' 'Because I did not know who still had it.' Nara laid the keys in a row. The tideglass needle trembled. Far above them, the silent Mourning Bell began to shed drops of black water.

They climbed to the bell chamber together. The Harbor Council had covered the mechanism with a plate bearing its seal. Tomas had scratched instructions beneath the plate, where no official would think to look. Nara cleaned away the salt with her sleeve. The bell could return every stolen name to the city. It could not return the people. Once the bell rang, the borrowed protection would end, and the streets would face the tide again.

'Then your father can't come home,' Jun said. He sounded ashamed, as though he had made it true by saying it. 'I know,' Nara answered, although until that moment she had not allowed herself to know. Elias looked away. Below them, the voice began to sing the song Tomas had used when storms frightened her. It missed the last line. She had forgotten the last line too.

Nara put the third key into the bell's heart, but she did not turn it. 'We have until the autumn tide,' she said. 'How long?' Jun asked. The tideglass needle struck the top of its case. From the harbor came the scrape of boats lifting against their ropes. Elias raised the empty lamp. For the first time, a pale flame appeared inside it. 'Long enough to warn them,' he said. 'If we begin now.'

documents.title: 03화 · 돌아온 이름들
paragraphs: They began with the houses nearest the harbor. Jun ran ahead, banging on shutters, while Nara told the waking families to leave their cellars and climb to the upper streets. Some believed her because she carried her father's tools. Others believed the water gathering around her boots. At the council hall, the doors remained shut. Elias left his lamp on the steps, and its thin light showed a tide mark higher than the handle.

At Nara's shop, Jun stopped beside the stove. 'You told me to keep it lit,' he said. The fire was still burning. Water had reached the legs of the workbench, and a box of brass fittings floated beneath it. Nara took down her father's coat, then put it back. 'Let it warm whoever comes through the door.' She rescued his notebook instead. Some things could be carried. Others had to be left doing their work.

By dawn, the upper streets were crowded with wet blankets, angry questions and children sleeping against strangers. Mrs. Vale stood among them, visible only when the harbor lamps flickered. She looked neither young nor restored. She looked tired. 'I wanted someone to remember my son,' she told Nara. 'Not to lose another child for him.' Then the lamp steadied, and the place where she had stood was empty.

Nara returned to the tower with Elias. Jun stayed above the harbor to help the families count their children. In the archive, the Grey Register had opened to a fresh page. Her name waited there, written beneath her father's. The offered exchange had never been a rescue. It had been a vacancy. She laid Tomas's notebook beside the book and did not touch either page.

At the Mourning Bell, Elias held the lamp while Nara turned the third key. The mechanism resisted, then moved with the weary click of a lock unused for years. From below came her father's voice, small and almost ordinary. 'Don't leave me.' Nara kept her hand on the key. 'My father wouldn't ask me to pay with someone else's life.' She turned it the rest of the way.

The first stroke shook salt from the rafters. The second carried across Greyhaven, through locked doors and crowded streets. At the third, Nara remembered Ada laughing at a broken umbrella outside her father's shop. Elias sat down before his knees could fail him. He did not speak. Names returned in fragments: a hand passing bread, a quarrel on a stair, a lullaby with its missing last line. The dead stayed dead. The city remembered whom it had lost.

The water rose after the bell stopped. It broke the council hall windows and filled the lower market, but the upper streets held. By afternoon, Jun brought word that the boats had carried the last families to safety. His borrowed scarf was gone. He had tied it to a railing to mark the safe path. Nara wanted to ask for it back, then pictured its bright strip above the water and said nothing.

That evening, she found Elias repairing a harbor lamp on the first dry step below the tower. 'Mr. Ward,' she said, 'will you still be the Ferryman?' He considered the question. 'Someone must help them cross. There will be ordinary boats now.' Nara opened her father's notebook to a clean page and wrote her own name. Beneath it she recorded the lamps that needed mending. When darkness came, Greyhaven had no borrowed light. It had the light they could make.
